newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel backs converting debt to euro in 1999.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel backs converting debt to euro in 1999.

text.p: Juergen Stark, state secretary in the German finance ministry, on Tuesday said Finance Minister Theo Waigel had agreed to his proposal that existing debt should be converted into euros from January 1, 1999.
"Waigel said he wants to," Stark said in response to a question. "That means it is effectively decided."
The decision would still have to be approved by parliament.
"But the political signal has been set," Stark added.
He announced last week at a Bundesbank news conference that he planned to propose to Waigel that existing debt should be converted into the new single currency from its launch date.
Bonn has long agreed that new debt issued after the euro's launch will be denominated in the new currency.
But France had paved the way for a conversion of existing debt as well, partly as a vote of confidence in the new single currency.
The French move raised fears in Germany that its financial centre could lose out after the switch to the euro.
The German banking association (BdB), which has long campaigned for outstanding debt to be converted quickly to the euro once it is established, welcomed the news.
"The early conversion will create a liquid market in federal government euro paper," it said in a statement.

"That means there is a good basis for large foreign institutional investors in particular to continue to invest in German paper in future. The federal government will retain its position as a benchmark issuer within monetary union."
Stark justified the plans to follow France's lead by saying that competition between financial centres would indeed become more intense once the euro was in place.

"If we did not do this, it would lead to a split market for German government paper. Neither segment would have sufficient liquidity," he said, referring to the new debt issued after 1999 and the existing debt if this had been left in marks.
"Ultimately, this decision will lead to an improvement in borrowing conditions for the government," he added.
Waigel's decision applies to issues made by the federal government itself and by government agencies.
The banking association said it hoped that private issuers would now also decide to convert paper into euros from the launch date for the currency.

Notes and coins in the new euro will not be issued until 2002. In the intervening period between this date and the launch there is no compulsion to use the new currency but the option is open to users in most areas.
